Repiping in Sarasota, FL

Repeated leaks, polybutylene pipe or rusty water? A whole-house repipe replaces the supply lines for good. SRQ Leak Pros connects you with a local repipe pro.

Call (941) 393-1012
  • Sarasota & Manatee counties
  • Service lines, slabs, sewers & pools
  • Homes, condos & businesses
  • Independent local providers

Quick answer: Repiping in Sarasota replaces a home's old water supply pipes, usually with PEX or copper, routed through walls and the attic instead of under the slab. It makes sense for polybutylene, galvanized steel or copper with repeated pinhole or slab leaks. Most repipes take a few days.

A repipe is a big job, but it solves a big problem. When a home's supply pipes are failing everywhere, fixing one leak at a time means more holes in drywall and more water damage. A repipe swaps all of it at once. In many Sarasota slab homes, the new lines run overhead, so future leaks won't hide under the floor.

Signs your home may need a repipe

SignWhat it often means
Gray plastic pipe marked PBPolybutylene, a known failure risk
Rusty or brown water, low pressureCorroding galvanized steel
Green spots or pinhole leaks on copperCopper wall thinning
Two or more slab leaksAging copper under the slab
Banging pipes and leaking jointsStress from water hammer or high pressure
A remodel that opens wallsA good time to replace old pipe

What a whole-house repipe includes

  • An inspection of current pipe material and layout
  • A written plan showing the new pipe routes
  • The permit and inspections
  • New hot and cold supply lines to each fixture
  • New angle stops and supply connectors at each fixture
  • A new main shut-off valve and, if needed, a pressure reducing valve
  • Pressure testing before walls are closed
  • Drywall patching, if quoted
  • Disposal or abandonment of the old pipe

Pipe materials compared

MaterialStrengthsWatch-outs
PEXFlexible, fewer fittings, resists scale and corrosionMust be kept out of direct sunlight
Copper (Type L)Long track record, heat tolerantHigher cost; can pinhole in some water
CPVCRigid plastic used for hot and cold linesCan turn brittle with age and heat

Wikipedia notes that CPVC is used for hot and cold water delivery pipes and is deemed safe for potable water. PEX is used mostly in building pipework and domestic water piping.

Polybutylene, galvanized and copper: why they fail

Polybutylene was used in several million U.S. and Canadian homes from about 1978 to 1997. Leaks and breaks led to a class action lawsuit, Cox v. Shell Oil, settled for $1 billion. The pipe can break down when exposed to chlorinated water, especially at fittings. It is no longer accepted by U.S. building codes. Read more in polybutylene pipes in Florida.

Galvanized steel is coated in zinc. Over decades, the inside rusts and narrows, which lowers pressure and can tint water brown.

Copper lasts a long time in many homes, but water chemistry, high flow and sand can thin the walls. Small holes called pinhole leaks often show up in clusters. See pinhole leaks in copper pipes.

How a repipe works, step by step

  1. Inspect. The pro confirms pipe types, fixture count and access points.
  2. Plan routes. New lines are mapped through the attic and walls, avoiding the slab.
  3. Permit. The permit is pulled before work starts.
  4. Open small access holes. Neat cuts are made in drywall where the pipe needs to pass.
  5. Run new pipe. Hot and cold lines are run to each fixture, often from a central manifold with PEX.
  6. Connect and test. Fixtures are reconnected and the system is pressure tested.
  7. Inspect. The local inspector signs off.
  8. Patch. Drywall is patched and the old lines are capped or removed.

What affects the cost

No price is quoted here, because repipes vary a lot by home. These factors drive the estimate:

  • Number of bathrooms, fixtures and the home's square footage
  • Pipe material chosen
  • One-story or two-story layout, and attic access
  • Drywall and paint repair included or not
  • Permit and inspection fees
  • Whether the water heater or main shut-off is also replaced

For one named data point, Angi's slab leak cost guide shows that a single slab repair averages about $2,300. If you've had more than one, compare that total with a repipe quote.

DIY vs. calling a pro

A repipe is not a DIY job. It needs a permit, pressure testing and connections at every fixture. You can help by checking your pipe type: look at exposed pipe near the water heater, under sinks or at the main shut-off. Gray plastic marked "PB" points to polybutylene.

Florida licensing and insurance notes

A repipe is plumbing work, so the provider should hold a Florida plumbing contractor license. Check the license number on the DBPR license search. Some insurers in Florida ask about polybutylene or galvanized pipe when writing or renewing a policy. Ask your agent how your pipe type affects coverage.

Local note

Local note: many homes built in North Port, Venice and Bradenton during the 1980s and 1990s may have polybutylene. Older cottages in Nokomis can still have galvanized supply lines.

Repiping questions

How long does a whole-house repipe take?

Many single-family repipes take two to five days, depending on size, layout and drywall repair. Water is usually off only for part of each day.

Is PEX or copper better for a repipe?

Both can work well. PEX is flexible and resists corrosion, while copper has a long track record. Ask the pro why they recommend one for your home.

Can I live in my home during a repipe?

Usually, yes. Most pros restore water at the end of each workday. Expect some dust and drywall cuts.

How do I know if I have polybutylene pipe?

Look for gray, sometimes blue or black, plastic pipe near the water heater, under sinks or at the main shut-off. It is often stamped PB.

Does a repipe include the service line?

Not always. The yard service line is often a separate job. Ask whether it is included or quote it as a water line replacement.
